input:
Organisations across every sector are increasingly recognising that the buildings they occupy represent a powerful and largely untapped opportunity in the journey towards lower energy costs and reduced carbon emissions, and the roof is perhaps the clearest example of this untapped potential. This proposal explores the opportunity presented by a rooftop solar installation for the organisation's building and seeks approval to move forward to the detailed design stage, which is the essential next step in turning an attractive concept into a well-defined and deliverable project. Rooftop solar is a proven, mature, and increasingly cost-effective technology, and generating electricity on site offers a wide range of benefits, from reduced exposure to rising and unpredictable grid prices, through to a visible demonstration of environmental responsibility that resonates with staff, customers, and stakeholders alike. In the pages that follow, the case for the installation is set out in full, the costs are presented transparently, a schedule for taking the project forward is described, and the specific decision that is being requested at this stage is clearly stated.

## Case

The case for installing solar generation on the roof is built on several mutually reinforcing strands. First and foremost, there is the financial strand: the building consumes electricity throughout the day, and electricity generated on the roof is consumed on site, offsetting purchases from the grid at the full price the organisation pays for its supply. In a market where prices have risen sharply and remain difficult to predict, the ability to generate a portion of the organisation's electricity at a cost that is fixed once the installation is built offers valuable protection and makes an important contribution to budget stability. Alongside the financial strand sits the environmental strand: every unit of solar electricity used in the building is a unit that does not need to be generated elsewhere, and this directly reduces the carbon emissions associated with the organisation's operations, supporting its broader sustainability ambitions and enhancing its reputation with the growing number of customers and partners who take environmental performance seriously. There is also a practical strand that is sometimes overlooked. The roof is an asset the organisation already owns, insures, and maintains, and at present it performs no function beyond sheltering the building. Putting it to work avoids the considerable cost and complexity of finding, acquiring, and preparing land for a ground-mounted alternative, and it places the generation directly at the point of use, minimising losses and connection complexity. Finally, there is a strategic strand: organisations that act early on on-site generation position themselves well for a future in which carbon reporting, building performance standards, and energy costs are all likely to move in directions that reward those who have already invested. It is important to acknowledge, however, that a strong general case is not the same thing as a proven case for this particular roof, and the detailed design stage is the mechanism by which the general case is tested against the realities of the building's orientation, shading, structure, and electrical infrastructure, ensuring that the eventual construction decision is grounded in evidence.

## Costs

The estimated capital cost of the rooftop solar installation is $785k, and the proposal is appraised over a 7-year appraisal horizon. This figure should be understood as a carefully prepared estimate at the proposal stage, assembled from budget pricing and experience of comparable installations, rather than as a fixed or guaranteed price. No contractor has yet been appointed, and it would be misleading to present the estimate as anything firmer than it is; one of the central purposes of the detailed design stage is to transform this indicative figure into a set of competitively tendered prices that can be relied upon. The estimate is comprehensive in its scope, embracing the solar panels and the mounting system by which they are fixed to the roof, the inverters and associated electrical equipment, the cabling and connection works that link the installation to the building's electrical distribution and to the wider grid, the protective devices and metering that a safe and compliant connection requires, the surveys, design work, and approvals that the project needs, and the costs of managing the project through installation, testing, and commissioning. The appraisal that accompanies the proposal balances this capital cost against the value of the electricity the installation is expected to produce across the 7-year horizon, net of the ongoing costs of running it, which include routine inspection, cleaning of the panels, monitoring of performance, insurance, and maintenance of the electrical equipment over time. Because the value of the output depends on future electricity prices, and the output itself depends on the weather and on the characteristics of the roof, the results of the appraisal are necessarily subject to uncertainty, and they are presented as a sound basis for deciding whether the project deserves to proceed to design, rather than as a precise prediction of the financial returns that will ultimately be achieved.

## Schedule

Subject to approval, the project will start one quarter after approval is given, and it will unfold through a logical sequence of stages, each building on the one before. The opening stage is the detailed design itself, in which the precise layout of the panels on the roof is determined, the load-bearing capacity of the roof structure is verified through survey and engineering assessment, the electrical design is developed in full, and the arrangements for connecting the installation to the grid are discussed and agreed with the relevant network operator. In parallel with this design work, the project will pursue whatever consents and approvals are required, so that momentum is maintained and the project is not delayed unnecessarily at a later point. Following the completion of the design, and subject to a separate and subsequent decision to proceed to construction, the project will move into procurement, with equipment ordered and an installation contractor selected through a competitive tendering process based on the completed design. The physical installation will then be carried out in a manner carefully planned to minimise disruption to the building and its occupants, with the works on the roof and the works to the electrical systems coordinated so that the building can continue to function normally throughout. The programme concludes with testing and commissioning, during which the installation is thoroughly checked and demonstrated to perform as intended, and with a formal handover of the documentation, monitoring arrangements, and maintenance information to the team who will be responsible for the installation in operation. The schedule is subject to a number of risks, most notably the time required to secure the grid connection, any strengthening work that the structural survey may identify as necessary, and the effect of poor weather on work at roof level, and the detailed design stage will clarify the programme in respect of these factors.

## Decision requested

The decision that is now requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, and it is essential that the scope of this decision is properly understood by everyone involved. Granting this approval authorises the design stage and the work that goes with it, including the surveys, the engineering design, the application for a grid connection, and the preparation of a complete and tender-ready definition of the works. It does not authorise construction, and it does not commit the organisation to building the installation; that commitment would only arise from a further decision, taken once the design is complete and firm prices are available. When the project returns for that decision, it will bring with it tendered prices to replace the current estimate of $785k, an updated appraisal across the 7-year horizon, and a clarified programme, allowing the construction decision to be taken on a firm and transparent basis. If, on the other hand, the detailed design reveals that the installation would be significantly less attractive than the proposal stage currently suggests, the project can be brought to a close at that point, with the organisation's exposure limited to the cost of the design work itself and with the benefit of a body of survey and design information that would remain valuable for any future consideration of the roof. Decision makers are therefore invited to approve the move to detailed design, commencing one quarter after approval, in the knowledge that the construction decision remains entirely separate and still to come.
target:
A rooftop solar installation is proposed for the building, and approval is requested to proceed to detailed design. The estimated capital cost is $785k, appraised over a 7-year horizon. The requested approval is for design only; construction is a separate decision, taken later against tendered prices. Work starts one quarter after approval.

## Case

Solar generation on the roof is used in the building that carries it. Each unit generated on site is a unit not bought from the grid, and its value is the retail price the organisation pays for electricity. Once built, the installation has no fuel cost, so the price of its output is fixed by the capital and running costs already committed, in a budget otherwise set by a market the organisation cannot influence. Output varies with the weather but is predictable in aggregate from year to year, and it is produced during the day, when the building is occupied and consuming. The environmental effect follows from the same displacement: grid electricity carries the emissions of the generation behind it, and electricity generated on the roof and used below it does not. The roof is the other half of the case. It is owned, insured, and maintained already, and it currently does nothing but shelter the building. Generation placed on it needs no land, and the point of generation is the point of use. These arguments establish that rooftop generation deserves examination; they do not establish the value of this installation. Output depends on how much of the roof is usable, how it faces, and what shades it. Cost depends on the structure beneath the covering and on the connection the network operator allows. Neither can be known from the general case. Detailed design exists to measure them, and the strength of the general case is the reason the measurement is worth paying for before the construction question is put. The match between generation and demand deserves emphasis, because it is what makes the value side of the case robust in a way the cost side is not: the building uses electricity through the working day, the array produces through the same hours, and the self-consumed share of the output is therefore high by construction rather than by assumption. The exported remainder earns less, and the design will state the split the roof and the load imply.

## Costs

The capital cost is estimated at $785k, with a 7-year appraisal horizon. The scope inside the estimate is the panels and the mounting system that fixes them to the roof, the inverters, the cabling and connection works to the building's distribution system and the grid, protection and metering equipment, surveys, design and approvals, and project management through installation, testing, and commissioning. The estimate is a proposal-stage figure. No contractor is named in it and no tender stands behind any part of it; it is assembled from budget pricing and comparable installations, and its uncertainty is the uncertainty of that basis. Against the capital cost, the appraisal sets the value of the expected generation over the horizon, less the running costs of inspection, panel cleaning, performance monitoring, insurance, and maintenance of the electrical equipment. The value side of the appraisal is uncertain for two distinct reasons: the generation depends on the roof and the weather, and its price depends on electricity prices over the horizon. The detailed design attacks the cost side and the generation side together — survey and design fix the scope and the expected output, and a tender converts the estimate into prices offered competitively for that fixed scope. The construction decision should rest on the tendered figure and on the refreshed appraisal, not on the proposal-stage numbers. Two features of the running costs are worth stating at this stage. The electrical components of the installation have shorter service lives than the panels and will need attention within the life of the project, and the cost of that attention belongs in the appraisal rather than in a later maintenance budget. The panels themselves carry no moving parts, and their upkeep is inspection and cleaning rather than repair.

## Schedule

The programme starts one quarter after approval. Detailed design is the first stage: the panel layout is settled, the roof structure is surveyed and assessed for the loads imposed on it, the electrical design is completed, and the grid connection is applied for and agreed with the network operator. Consents are pursued in parallel with the design, so that approval processes do not become the constraint once the design is finished. Procurement belongs after the construction decision: equipment is ordered and an installer appointed by competitive tender against the completed design. Installation is planned around the building in use; roof works and electrical works are coordinated so that normal occupation continues, and the disruptive elements are placed where they disturb least. Testing and commissioning follow, in which the installation is demonstrated against the design, and handover passes the documentation, the monitoring arrangements, and the maintenance requirements to the team that will operate it. The programme carries three named risks. The connection agreement is in the network operator's hands and may set the pace. The structural survey may require strengthening works that were not in the scope. Weather can halt roof works. The design stage converts the first two risks from possibilities into facts with prices and durations attached, and the programme offered with the construction decision will show them. Building users are told the programme before the roof works begin, and the noisy stages are placed where occupation is lightest; the obligation runs the other way as well, in that access the design assumes has to be kept available while the works proceed. The design stage also fixes the evidence the commissioning must produce, so that handover is a comparison against stated requirements and not a general inspection.

## Decision requested

Approval is requested to proceed to detailed design, and the scope of the approval should be read exactly. It authorises surveys, engineering design, the grid connection application, and a tender-ready definition of the works. It does not authorise construction, and no commitment to build arises from it. The construction decision returns to this forum with tendered prices in place of the estimate, the appraisal over the 7-year horizon refreshed on the designed scope, and a programme that reflects the survey findings and the connection terms. Taken then, the construction decision rests on firm prices and measured characteristics of the roof. If the design instead shows the installation to be materially worse than the proposal indicates, the project closes at design stage; the cost incurred is the design cost, and the survey and design record remains as an asset for any future proposal affecting the roof. The request is therefore for the design stage only, starting one quarter after approval, with construction expressly reserved for a later decision. Deferral is the remaining alternative, and its cost should be stated plainly: the roof, the prices, and the connection terms available now are not held open by delay, and a later proposal would start again from survey. Nothing in the design stage forecloses that choice, but the choice should be made knowing that the present figures lapse with it.
